title: Be one
hook: no more arguing about what a good person is; be one (Meditations 10.16)
carry: show it by what it produces

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayaz and his old sandals, and the courtiers who dug and found nothing. Your line was the old shoes.

You can spend a whole evening talking about exercise. Which plan is best, which app, which shoes, what the latest study says. At the end of the evening, you've walked about forty steps, from the couch to the fridge. Planning to be good can feel almost as nice as being good, and it's much less work. For weeks now, Marcus has been thinking hard about how to live. In Book Ten, he seems to catch himself doing just that, and he writes himself one short, blunt sentence.
screen: `AN EVENING ABOUT EXERCISE.` → `FORTY STEPS TO THE FRIDGE.` → `BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Book Ten, section sixteen. In George Long's translation: "No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such." Stop talking about what a good person is. Be one. You might hear this as a strange thing for Marcus to write; the Meditations is full of thinking about how to be good. But that's the point. It doesn't read like a book written to be admired. It reads like a notebook of reminders, from a man trying to act better the next morning. For the Stoics, philosophy wasn't a topic. It was a way of life. Epictetus, whose sayings Marcus read, made the same point in his Handbook. Don't explain your principles at dinner; eat as a person should. Sheep don't bring their grass to the shepherd to show how much they've eaten. They digest it, and it comes out as wool and milk. Show your principles by what they produce. There's relief in this, too. You don't have to settle every question first, or finish the book, or pass the test, or become an expert in goodness. Right now, there's one kind thing within reach. Do that. Marcus has been saying pieces of this all along: the vine that gives its grapes, stay simple, dig within. Today he just drops the explanation. Your line: show it by what it produces.
screen: `NO LONGER TALK ABOUT IT.` · `A NOTEBOOK, NOT A MONUMENT.` · `SHEEP DON'T SHOW THEIR GRASS.` · then, large: `BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Let the questions about what's right go quiet, and let one simple good act come to mind, something you could do in the next hour: a dish, a message, a kind word, a bit of patience. Don't plan a speech about it. Just see yourself doing it, and rest there.
Be one. Marcus told himself to stop talking about what a good person ought to be, and simply be one. Today's word.
Your line: show it by what it produces. Wool and milk, not grass. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: For the Stoics philosophy was a way of life, and readers of Marcus often use this line to turn from reading and discussion to one concrete good act.

fork.reveal: no longer talk at all about the kind of man a good man ought to be, but be such.

original.note: Greek: good. Marcus's word for the person he'd rather be than describe.

trapdoor: what it means: goodness is shown by doing it, not by defining it.
what a scholar hears: the ancient view of philosophy as a way of life, and Epictetus's image in the Handbook (46) of sheep producing wool, not showing their grass.

recall: a former slave who became a Stoic teacher

notes: Epictetus, Enchiridion 46 (don't talk about principles at a banquet; sheep and grass): paraphrased. Confirm.
